summary:
Project A.R.E.S. 2.0 asks one question: can YOU keep four astronauts alive on Mars for 50 sols? 
Every kilogram you pack into your Starship is a kilogram you can never take back, so choose wisely, launch, build a habitat on the Red Planet, and survive whatever space throws at you. Real solar storms from NASA’s DONKI space weather database become live in-game hazards, while a Gemini-powered AI Flight Director writes fresh mission objectives, reviews your decisions and springs surprise problems on you, so no two missions are ever the same. 
Hands-on mini-games like Shard Collector, Shard Memory and Fragment Catcher build the skills junior astronauts need, and a two-player crew mode lets you invite a friend (they have to accept!) and run the mission together, live, with a shared pause. Wrapped in a retro terminal style with falling-code rain, it plays free in your browser and installs on Android, iOS, Windows, Mac and Chrome. 
Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to teach real space science through play. Ready, Commander? Pack light, think fast, and bring everyone home.
details:
Overview

PROJECT A.R.E.S. 2.0 (Advanced Resource & Environment Simulator) is a single-file browser game that trains junior astronauts to plan, build and survive a 50-sol Mars mission, made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. You pack a Starship, fit out its interior, land at Arcadia Planitia and keep a crew of four alive.

The game teaches one idea over and over: every resource is linked to another. Oxygen needs water, water needs power, power needs mass, and mass is limited. Good choices before launch decide how hard the surface is.

  • Who it is for: students and first-time space fans. A guided Cadet mode and a free-text Flight Director mode cover both levels.
  • Where it runs: any modern browser, from one HTML file. It can also be installed as an app.
  • Goal: survive 50 sols with oxygen, water and food above zero, and finish the mission objectives Mission Control sets.
  • Look and feel: a green retro terminal, with canvas-drawn cutscenes and mini-games.

Main attraction

The main attraction is the packing-to-survival loop: what you choose to launch with is what you live with on Mars. Everything else in the game supports that loop.

  1. The mass budget. You get 24,000 kg and 60 m³ of cargo space. Each item has a weight, a volume, power use and ports it needs.
  2. A real interior to build. You place modules on three decks (Habitat & Crew, Science & Greenhouse, Utility & EVA Yard) and connect the ports each one needs (power, water, oxygen, methane, light).
  3. Live consequences. Power, oxygen, water, food, radiation, morale and methane all update every sol, so a bad layout shows up as numbers falling.
  4. Real space weather. The game reads NASA's DONKI feed and uses a real solar event to time a hazard. If the feed is offline, it simulates one.
  5. An AI trainer. Gemini, or a local Ollama model as backup, writes mission objectives, judges typed fixes and speaks problem alerts.
  6. SHIP DRIVING. A separate big button starts a deep-space flight with planets to dock at, debris to dodge and ship faults that stop the ship until you fix them.
  7. Cinematics. A launch cutscene, a landing and an ending sequence, all drawn live.
  8. Co-op. Up to three friends can join the same mission over a peer-to-peer link.

Key to understanding it all

The whole game fits in one chain: mass limits what you carry, what you carry limits your power, and power limits your life support. Read the three tabs as three stages of that chain.

Glossary

Sol : One Martian day. The mission runs 50 sols; the clock ticks on its own

Manifest : The list of everything loaded onto the Starship

Ports : Connections (PWR, H2O, O2, CH4, LIGHT) a module needs before it

: produces or consumes anything

ISRU : Making resources on Mars (ice drill for water, electrolyzer for oxygen)

Methalox / CH4: Methane fuel reserve; fuel cells burn it for power

Battery buffer : Stored power that carries you through the night and dust storms

Shielding : Protection from radiation; falls during solar events

Morale Crew mood (0 to 100). Low morale triggers problems; some actions spend it :

EVA : Going outside. Needs an Airlock or Suit Locker; collects samples

Cadet mode : Easy mode: pick one of three fixes for each problem

Flight Director mode Hard mode: type your own fix and an AI or local judge scores it

Mini-game : Short arcade game that gives crew morale or supplies

Sol clock hold : The sol counter pauses while a mini-game or problem is open

Safety margin to remember: the Starship launches with only 10 sols of emergency O₂, water and food. Without bulk reserves or production systems, the crew runs out on Sol 11.

Step-by-step walkthrough

A full run takes you from the start screen to either MISSION COMPLETE or CREW EXTINGUISHED.

  1. Start screen. Choose START MISSION for solo play. The other buttons are MULTIPLAYER, AI SETUP (check Gemini or Ollama), DOWNLOAD APP and HOW TO PLAY. Read HOW TO PLAY the first time.
  2. Pick a training mode. CADET gives guided choices. FLIGHT DIRECTOR makes you type your own fixes. You can switch on the manifest screen.
  3. Tab 01, Manifest & Mass Budget. Watch payload mass and cargo volume left. Add power, life support, food, shielding, EVA and science items, then bulk reserves (oxygen, water, food, fuel cans, methane). Use the category filters to find things.
  4. Check the pre-flight notice. Remember the 10-sol emergency supply. You need reserves or ISRU production before you seal.
  5. Seal the manifest. Press SEAL MANIFEST. Mission Control then issues secondary objectives (the AI drafts them).
  6. Tab 02, Interior Configuration. Drag each item into a slot on its deck. Connect the ports it needs. Items you could not place are listed as unplaced. Items that need pressurized space, such as the CO₂ Scrubber, must go in the Habitat deck.
  7. Launch. Start the mission. The launch cutscene plays, then the landing at Arcadia Planitia.
  8. Tab 03, Surface Operations. The sol clock starts. Each sol the game recalculates power, oxygen, water, food, radiation and morale.
  9. React to problems. A problem box opens and the sol clock pauses. Solve it in Cadet or Flight Director style (see Problems and decisions).
  10. Keep the reserves up. Use ADD FUEL for the generator, the Morale Bank for boosts, and mini-games for morale.
  11. Collect science. With an airlock or suit locker, EVA collects up to 5 samples. A spectrometer analyses them. Three analyzed samples can reveal an anomaly, and RUN CONFIRMATION PROTOCOL then confirms life.
  12. Optional: SHIP DRIVING. Press the big button for a deep-space run. It advances 10 sols and costs supplies (see Ship Driving).
  13. Reach Sol 50. Survive past Sol 50 for MISSION COMPLETE and the ending cinematic. If oxygen, water or food hits zero in a way that kills the crew, the failure cutscene plays and the mission ends at that sol.

Mini-games and Ship Driving

There are three arcade mini-games and one big-button flight. All of them hold the sol clock while you play, and none can be opened during a problem.

Shard Collector : Mini-games row, Surface Ops. Collect falling shards.

Reward: crew morale. Cooldown: 3 sols.

Shard Memory : Mini-games row. Match shards from memory.

Reward: crew morale. Cooldown: 3 sols.

Fragment Catcher : Mini-games row. Catch fragments outside (EVA suit-up costs 4 kg O2;

a habitat window works with no airlock).

Reward: crew morale. Cooldown: 3 sols.

Ship Driving : Big button above the mini-games row. Fly a deep-space route.

Reward: loot crate, 10 sols pass. Cooldown: about 4 minutes of real time.

How SHIP DRIVING works

  1. Press the big ▶ MARS TRANSIT: SHIP DRIVING button.
  2. Steer with UP/DOWN or W/S, or drag on the screen. Stay inside the dashed route.
  3. Near a planet or moon, hold SPACE (or the HOLD TO DOCK button) for about 1.5 seconds to collect loot: oxygen, water, food or fuel. A cargo crate collects it.
  4. Dodge the debris. Each hit costs 1 hull point (3 in total) and a little oxygen; time off the route costs water and oxygen.
  5. Ship faults. Two or three times during the flight, the ship stops. A fault panel opens (coolant leak, hull puncture, CO₂ alarm, solar storm and others). In Cadet mode, choose one of three fixes. In Flight Director mode, type your fix. Each wrong answer costs 2 kg O₂, and running out of tries costs 1 hull point.
  6. Press CONTINUE FLIGHT (or Enter) and the ship flies on from where it stopped.
  7. At the sector exit you get a summary. The run advances 10 sols and uses about 35 L water, 20 food and about 1% of battery capacity. Open the cargo crate icon to store the loot.

SKIP TRANSIT ends the run with no stops made.

Problems and decisions

Every problem pauses the sol clock, opens a red problem box and is read aloud. There are six core problems, plus AI-written complications and anomalies that Mission Control can add during sols 4 to 26.

Payload overweight : Lander too heavy for descent.

Fixes: drop Hydroponics, burn methane, or offload rations.

CO2 scrubber saturation: CO2 rising, crew headaches.

Fixes: vent cabin (costs O2), max regen (costs power), or use the storm shelter.

Water recycler rupture : Clean water production offline.

Fixes: cannibalize the ISRU drill, ration water, or boil down (drains batteries).

Solar array dust blanket Output down 60% :

Fixes: EVA brush-off (needs airlock), battery buffer, or overdrive fission.

Crew morale diminished : Exhausted, arguing crew.

Fixes: Shard Memory night, comfort rations, or push on (worse).

Micrometeorite puncture: Hab pressure falling.

Fixes: seal the section, brick patch (needs printer), or EVA repair.

Modes

Cadet mode. You pick one of three fixes. Some are locked until you own the hardware they need, and each shows its cost. Every option trades one resource for another.

Flight Director mode. You type your own fix. Empty or off-topic messages are rejected. The AI judge (Gemini or Ollama) reads your answer and decides whether it is safe and plausible; if no AI is running, a local keyword judge accepts a fix that names the right actions. An improvised fix costs 10 morale. A weak answer can trigger a complication.

The rule to remember: there is no free fix. If a choice looks free, look again at what it spends.

Do's

  • Do pack bulk reserves of oxygen, water and food, or ISRU production, before you seal the manifest.
  • Do add a power source that survives a dust storm (Kilopower fission) and a battery buffer for the night.
  • Do put the CO₂ Scrubber and other pressure-bound items on the Habitat deck.
  • Do connect every port an item needs (power, water, oxygen, methane, light), or it produces nothing.
  • Do include an Airlock or Suit Locker, a spectrometer and comms if you want the science and communication objectives.
  • Do include a Medical Bay, exercise rig and hydroponics for morale on a long mission.
  • Do read the cost line on every fix before you click it.
  • Do use the Morale Bank and mini-games when morale is falling, but keep morale at least 5 above the cost of any boost.
  • Do check the cooldown on mini-games (3 sols) and SHIP DRIVING (about 4 minutes) before planning around them.
  • Do budget supplies for SHIP DRIVING: it advances 10 sols and uses water, food and power.
  • Do answer ship faults by naming the action and the system (for example, isolate the loop and switch to the backup).
  • Do save or keep the one HTML file, and use the same file on every device in multiplayer.

Don'ts

  • Don't seal the manifest with no reserves and no production. The crew runs out on Sol 11.
  • Don't rely on solar panels alone. A dust storm cuts their output to about 20%.
  • Don't forget that the fuel cell burns your methane reserve, and the generator only runs while it has fuel cans.
  • Don't overload the mass or volume budget; items you cannot afford simply do not fit.
  • Don't drop Hydroponics, the drill or other key hardware as a quick fix unless you have a plan to replace what it gave you.
  • Don't vent the cabin to clear CO₂ when oxygen is already low.
  • Don't start a mini-game or SHIP DRIVING while a problem is open; the game blocks it.
  • Don't start SHIP DRIVING when water or food is nearly gone; the run drains both and can leave you short.
  • Don't leave the dashed route or hit debris on purpose; both cost oxygen, water and hull.
  • Don't type empty, joke or off-topic answers to Flight Director problems; they are rejected.
  • Don't ignore low morale. It makes every problem harder.
  • Don't mix game files in multiplayer. A guest on a different version is refused by the host.

Multiplayer, tech notes and learning goals

Multiplayer. One player hosts and up to three guests join with a room code over a peer-to-peer link (PeerJS). Everyone sees the same mission. Guests send actions to the host, which runs the simulation. All players must use the same game file version, or the host refuses the join. SHIP DRIVING and the mini-games are started through the host's rules.

Tech notes.

  • One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and JavaScript; it also works as an installable web app.
  • Graphics are canvas drawings in a green CRT style, with no external image assets for the mini-games.
  • Data sources: NASA DONKI (space weather) with a simulated fallback.
  • AI: Gemini or a local Ollama model, with the other one as backup. The game works with no AI, using local judging.

Learning goals. Players practise budgeting mass and volume, seeing resource dependencies, planning for risk, choosing between trade-offs and explaining an engineering fix in plain words.

Thank you for your patience.
